title: Building a Lao Language LLM with Gemma 4: A Complete Guide
excerpt: How I fine-tuned Google's Gemma 4 E4B model to understand and generate Lao text — covering vocab surgery, continual pre-training, and supervised fine-tuning from scratch.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Lao is one of the most underrepresented languages in modern AI. With fewer than 100 million speakers and limited digital text resources, training a language model from scratch is impractical. Instead, I took a different approach: adapting Google's Gemma 4 E4B — a powerful 4-billion-active-parameter multimodal model — to understand and generate Lao text through a three-stage pipeline.

sections.title: Step 1 — Collect Lao Language Data
sections.body: The foundation of any language model is data. I collected Lao text from four main sources: Wikipedia dumps (lo.wikipedia.org), news and blog sites (KPL, Vientiane Times), banking domain documents (terms and conditions, FAQs, notices from IndochinaBank), and the FLORES-200 Lao benchmark set. After cleaning and deduplication, the corpus contained approximately 53,000 text samples covering ~17 million characters of natural Lao text.

sections.title: Step 2 — Tokenizer Audit and Vocab Surgery
sections.body: This was the most critical and technically challenging step. Gemma 4's original tokenizer was trained primarily on English and a handful of high-resource languages. For Lao, it fragmented nearly every word into UTF-8 byte sequences — a single Lao word like ນະຄອນ would become 9-12 tokens instead of 1-2. I audited the tokenizer, found that only 290 out of 31,569 common Lao tokens existed in the original vocabulary, and performed vocab surgery: training a new SentencePiece BPE tokenizer on the Lao corpus and injecting 28,022 new Lao tokens into Gemma 4's embedding layer. New token embeddings were initialized using a smart mean-of-subparts strategy.

sections.title: Step 3 — Continual Pre-Training (CPT)
sections.body: With the extended vocabulary in place, I ran continual pre-training on the Lao corpus. This phase teaches the model what the new Lao tokens actually mean by training it to predict the next token in Lao text. Using QLoRA (4-bit quantization + LoRA adapters) with Unsloth on a Vast.ai RTX 4090, training ran for 3 epochs over 9,945 steps (~17.5 hours). Loss dropped from 0.82 to 0.60, indicating the model successfully learned Lao language patterns.

sections.title: Step 4 — Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
sections.body: After CPT, the model could predict Lao text but could not follow instructions. SFT taught it to be a helpful assistant. I translated 3,000 Alpaca instruction-response pairs to Lao using Google Translate, converted them to Gemma chat format, and ran SFT for 3 epochs on the same RTX 4090. Training completed in just 49 minutes at a cost of $0.24. Final loss: 0.4275.

sections.title: Step 5 — Merge and Evaluate
sections.body: The CPT and SFT LoRA adapters were merged into the base model to create a standalone model: AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full. Testing showed that English responses remained accurate (The capital of Laos is Vientiane), while Lao responses generated fluent text but with factual errors — a known limitation of using machine-translated SFT data. Future work will focus on human-written Lao Q&A pairs and OCR pipeline integration.

sections.title: Lessons Learned
sections.body: 1. Vocab surgery is non-negotiable for low-resource languages — without it, training efficiency is terrible. 2. Cloud GPU costs matter: the entire CPT run cost ~$7 on Vast.ai RTX 4090. 3. SFT data quality matters more than quantity — 3,000 Google-translated pairs was not enough for factual accuracy. 4. Gemma 4 is a multimodal model — the same fine-tuned model can potentially do Lao OCR by processing document images. 5. Start small, iterate fast: the full pipeline from idea to working model took less than two weeks.

sections.title: What's Next
sections.body: The model is available publicly at AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full on HuggingFace. Next steps include collecting human-written Lao instruction pairs, integrating with a Lao OCR pipeline for document digitization, evaluating on the FLORES-200 Lao benchmark, and deploying via Ollama REST API for use in banking applications at IndochinaBank.
